raw_response:
I've been farming these 8 mu in Quzhou for 45 years, and with my agricultural college background, I tend to think in terms of targets and rates — though at my age and on this small plot, I've learned that the pocketbook always has the final say. My son works off-farm in Shijiazhuang, so it's just me and my wife running day-to-day operations. We have some income from his job, but I don't like depending on it for farm expenses. Eight mu is not much land, and every yuan I spend on inputs has to earn its way back.

For the winter wheat, I'm targeting about 480 kg/mu. I'll plant around October 10th — I've seen what happens when you plant too early and the wheat grows too tall before winter, or too late and tillering suffers. I'm using an improved semi-dwarf variety; the seed costs about 35 yuan per mu, but it's reliable. For fertilizer, I'm calculating 18 kg N/mu total. I'll put down 50 kg per mu of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer as a base before planting and work it in with the rotary tiller. Then at jointing in late March, I'll topdress with 20 kg per mu of urea — that gives me another 9 kg N or so. I used to do a third application at heading, but with urea prices where they are and only 8 mu to spread the cost over, I've dropped that. Phosphorus and potassium come mainly from the compound fertilizer: about 7.5 kg P and 5 kg K per mu. I'll irrigate three times — pre-winter to ensure good establishment, once at jointing, and once at heading. The pumping costs about 15 yuan per mu per irrigation, so that's roughly 360 yuan just for wheat water, but I learned in 2019 that skipping heading irrigation cost me nearly 80 kg/mu. That's a loss I can't afford on this scale. For pesticides, I'll use a pre-emergence herbicide and keep an eye out for powdery mildew or rust at heading — if I see it, I'll spray a fungicide once.

The summer maize is dictated by the turnaround window. I'll harvest wheat around June 10–12, and I need maize in the ground by June 15–16 at the latest. The season is too short for saved seed — I'll buy a single-cross hybrid at 55 yuan per mu. It pains me to pay that much for seed, but the yield advantage is 80–100 kg/mu over local open-pollinated varieties, so the math works out. For fertilizer, I'm targeting 16 kg N/mu, 5 kg P, and 4 kg K. Because the window is so tight, everything goes down at planting: 40 kg/mu of 18-10-8 compound plus 8 kg/mu of urea in the seed furrow. No split application — there's no time, and the maize growing season is short enough that one good dose usually carries it if the rains cooperate. I'll plan for one irrigation, probably at the big-flare or silking stage, but honestly I often get away with zero if July and August deliver decent rain. A second irrigation would cost another 120 yuan for the plot, and on 8 mu that margin matters. I'll use a pre-emergence herbicide and watch for corn borers — if I see damage, I'll spray insecticide, but I don't spray preventively anymore. Labor is mostly me and my wife, but I'll hire 2–3 days of help for harvest and bagging. At 65, hauling 50-kg grain bags is no longer something my back tolerates for long.

My total input cost this year will run about 4,200 yuan. That's a big chunk of our cash reserves, but with wheat at current prices and my yield targets, I should recover that and have enough left for household expenses. I don't optimize — I satisfice. I could probably push yields higher with more fertilizer and another maize irrigation, but the risk-reward on 8 mu doesn't justify it. I'd rather sleep soundly knowing I haven't bet everything on one season.
